subject: nineTailedKitsune
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: nine-tailed kitsune fox with spirit flames.
Style: high-fantasy anime.
reasoning:
I'm planning the structure for a single TypeScript module containing a nine-tailed kitsune fox with spirit flames, thinking through its pose, proportions, and scale before writing any code.

I'm now working out the skeleton: hips root, a spine chain of catmull-rom points running from rump to neck, plus later chains for neck, head, ears, legs, and nine fanned tail chains with flame effects at their tips, using the toon and glow kits for shading and glow materials.

Checking that spans match the names array length, I'm now thinking about the overall body loft, planning a single sweep path running from the rump through the chest up to the neck base, defined as a catmull curve through several body points.

Mapping out radius values along that path -- larger at the chest, tapering toward the rump and neck -- and linking the sweep to a bone chain covering hips, spine, and neck joints so the mesh deforms correctly.

Now I'm deciding on the kitsune's color palette, settling on a cream-white coat with vermilion markings and dark leg socks, plus blue-cyan spirit flame accents for the tail tips.

Defining the paint palette...

Writing body paint logic...

Now I'm planning the leg structure as limb chains—figuring out shoulder and target positions for the front legs with segment lengths for upper arm, forearm, and paw.

I'll just call both front and rear limbs "leg" with side suffixes "L"/"R" for left/right since left is +X. For the hind leg, I'm working out digitigrade segment lengths (thigh, shin, metatarsal) and bend directions, placing the hip root and foot target coordinates so the chain reaches naturally toward the ground.

Now I'm figuring out the joint naming for each leg chain (hip, knee, hock, paw) matching the number of segments and bend directions, then setting up varying sweep radii along each leg so the thigh is thicker than the paw.

Adding paw geometry now...

I'll root the front legs a bit closer, around x=±0.09, so they sprout naturally from the chest surface. For the head, I'm planning a skull-snout-jaw structure with cone-shaped cheek fur tufts, pointed triangular ears with red inner coloring, anime-style eye decals, a dark nose sphere, and red kumadori stripes beneath the eyes for a tengu-like mask effect.

I'm figuring out how to place facial markings using decals — using a region/local coordinate system defined by forward, up, and left offsets relative to the head joint, so I can position the forehead tomoe mark and other features intuitively without fighting raw coordinates.

Now I'm sketching the skull geometry itself: a scaled sphere positioned slightly forward and up for the head, then tapering into the snout using a frustum box shape for that blocky, low-poly fox look. I'm weighing whether a tapered lathe shape might give a smoother snout than the blocky frustum approach.

Writing sweep parameters...

Working through the jaw geometry, I'm adjusting the vertical offsets so the upper and lower jaw segments overlap slightly to form a closed mouth rather than leaving a visible gap, treating the lower jaw as a subtle chin shape beneath the snout.

Positioning the dark nose sphere near the snout tip, then working out the ear shapes as extruded flat triangles angled upward and outward using directional vectors for the outline axes.

Shaping the ear outline...

I'm working out the ear's local orientation and thickness direction using a cross product so the extrusion faces outward symmetrically for both left and right ears, then planning a smaller inset extrude for the inner ear coloring.

Pink inner ear with white fur tuft, and I'm setting up earL/earR joints parented to the head for rigging. I'm working out the outward tilt of the ear so the tip leans about 25° outward, keeping the axes reasonably orthogonal through the tip offset rather than the rotation itself.

Now I'm shaping the skull as a sphere part attached to the head bone, scaled non-uniformly along world axes to get the right width, height, and depth, and double-checking that scale accepts an array in this part system like the toon example does.

For the eyes, I'm placing them as decals on the skull surface using azimuth and elevation offsets, mirrored for left/right symmetry — computing where az 38° lands on the sphere's surface so the eye size fits near the snout bridge, keeping them slightly elevated for that anime fox look.

Checking whether the snout geometry overlaps the eye placement: tracing the snout's taper from forward 0.08 with shrinking radius, I find the eye at x=0.065 sits just outside the snout's edge at that depth, so it's not occluded — but it's close enough that I should push the snout start forward to 0.1 and shrink its starting radius to 0.06, while adjusting the eye azimuth to 45° for better clearance.

Now I'm working out the kumadori face markings — red stroke lines sweeping outward and back from the eyes, done as an SVG decal placed on the skull using hit-normal orientation, with a tapered swoosh path in a red tone (#e8452c), positioned below and behind the eye at roughly azimuth offset 62° and elevation -8°, scaled up from a 60-unit-wide viewBox to a 256px texture.

I'll drop the orientation obsession and just make the cheek marking a symmetric-ish forked swoosh, since exact mirroring isn't critical here. Next I'll add a forehead mark — a red teardrop or diamond shape placed at the top.

For the forehead decal, I'm sizing a flame-shaped teardrop texture with a gold dot accent, oriented along the hit normal which works fine at this elevation without degeneracy issues. Then for cheek fur, I'm placing a few small spikes manually around each cheek using local head-relative offsets to create outward-pointing tufts.

Working out the direction vectors and spike radius for chunky white cone shapes...

Now I'm adding cheek tufts with swept-back spikes, then building a neck ruff by placing a ring of spikes around the neck pointing back and down.

I also want a second ring near the chain point for layering, placing two rings at different t-values along the neck with slight rotation offsets. For the chest, I'm adding a tuft of spikes near the lower spine, restricting their angular range to the bottom half so they sweep downward and backward like a spiky bib.

Now I'm designing the nine tails fanning from the rump: each is a short curved chain with a thick, tapering radius profile for a fluffy look, and I'm spreading them in a fan pattern by varying yaw angle symmetrically from center outward while adjusting pitch so outer tails arc differently than the center one.

Naming joints `tail${i+1}_${k+1}` for rigging clarity, giving nine tails × four joints = 36, keeping total joint count safely under budget. I'm also shaping each tail with a tapered radius function so it starts thin, flares fluffy in the middle, then narrows to a point.

For coloring, I'm thinking a cream-white body with flame-colored tips, using banded gradients that shift from white to red-orange near the end, plus a zigzag fur-edge paint effect along the tail's silhouette to mimic kitsune fur texture.

Now I want to add floating spirit flames (hitodama) hovering above each tail tip -- building each as a crossed teardrop-shaped extrusion with soft glow to resemble a small flame.

Writing flame sweep and bone logic...

Now thinking about floating foxfire orbs scattered around the fox, hovering near tails and shoulders without dipping below floor level. Instead of random placement, I'll organize them into a ring halo above the back plus a wider circle of wisps at hip height, radius around 0.7.

Designing a wisp helper that builds each flame as a swept teardrop shape — round at the base, tapering to a point at the top, positioned in a spiral around the body with varying radius and height.

Actually I'll reverse the flame coloring so the hot core is pale white near the base and shifts through cyan to a violet-blue tip, layering bands at 0.4, 0.75, and 1.0, each with their own cloned material so the glow effect picks up the meshes properly. I'm keeping track of the flat color count to stay under the material budget.

For decorations, I'm swapping a shimenawa rope for a gold bell necklace with red tassels and magatama beads, then building a neck collar by taking a surface loop at a frame positioned along the neck's chain and sweeping it into a thin ring geometry.

I'm placing a gold bell sphere in front of the collar at a point offset slightly down and forward from the neck, attaching it as a stick decoration, with red tassels hanging below, and distributing small gold bead spheres evenly along the collar loop.

I'm skipping leg anklets and wrist rings to keep things within scope, but considering adding small gold cuff rings at the base of each tail for ornamentation.

Still writing tail ring placement...

Still working out orientation...

Now I'm designing the fan of nine tails, spreading their yaw angles across roughly 70 degrees from a shared base so they fluff out symmetrically, parameterizing each with a direction vector and starting point offset by u.

I'm sketching the fan shape with each tail arcing up and outward at varying elevation and yaw angles, steeper and more vertical in the center, drooping more horizontal toward the edges, then parameterizing each as a short multi-point curve computed by incrementing position along a changing elevation direction.

That height feels too tall relative to the fox body, so I'm scaling back the elevation angles and tail length to keep the proportions more believable, aiming for a tip around 1.3-1.4 meters instead of 1.56.

I'm also noticing the nine tails will clutter and overlap near the midpoint given their radius and angular spacing, so I'm shrinking the tail diameter from 0.2 to 0.15 and relying on the staggered elevations to keep them visually separated.

Widening the yaw spread to roughly ±78° should keep the fan fluffy without the outer tails colliding with the hind legs, since they stay elevated above the rump and clear the leg position behind the body.

I'm adjusting the tail base to sit slightly inside the body near the rump, with a smaller starting radius, then setting up each tail as a chain of catmull-spline joints parented to the hips so they sprout naturally from that region, naming each segment procedurally.

I'm reworking the point count for the tail curve to get the right number of joint spans, then sweeping each chain into a tube shape with keyed radii that taper toward a pointed tip, though I'm reconsidering whether the tips should be blunter and more rounded for a fluffier look.

Setting the circle cross-section sides and deciding to keep them smooth rather than faceted, then placing a small flame shape at each tail tip, anchored slightly above the tip position along its tangent direction.

Having the flames tilt outward alternately for a windswept look, with overall height around 1.8 against a 0.9 fox body length, keeping flames smaller toward the center. I'm also considering a crown flame on the forehead and a ring of floating orbs around the figure.

Now I'm working out the orb ring placement -- six wisps at alternating angles and radii around the origin, kept small and hovering above the ground, while checking that they don't collide with the fox's tail positioned at the back.

Tightening the angle to avoid overlap with the tail, I'm settling on a narrower spread so the wisps don't clash with the tail geometry. For surface details, I'm adding decorative flame-swirl decals on the shoulders and hips to give the creature some kitsune-style markings rather than a plain white body.

Setting up the decal placement logic...

Adding leg sock paint with zigzag boundaries...

Still writing whisker and rod code...

I'm also considering small cute details like tiny red eyebrow dots above the eyes using flat-colored spheres, and thinking about whether to skip a forehead gem decoration to keep things simple.

Now I'm sketching the lower jaw: fangs for teeth, a white jaw with no extra chin patch, and building the jaw bone as a sweep between two points near the head, tapering the width along its length with rounded caps.

For the upper snout, I'm placing another sweep that tapers radii toward the nose, adding a small scaled sphere at the tip to form the nose itself, then continuing to define where the lower jaw segment ends.

Checking the gap between upper and lower jaw curves across the parameter range to make sure they stay separated enough for the mouth opening to read correctly.

Now I'm working out the neck-to-head joint placement, making sure the skull center and front edge line up properly with where the neck terminates.

Checking head and ear heights against the shoulder, I adjust the neck end slightly lower to fix proportions for the fox shape. Then I'm plotting the spine sweep from rump to neck through a series of points, assigning radius values at each key to shape the body's taper.

Setting up the skeleton hierarchy now, defining the hips joint and a spine chain parented to it, built from the same curve points.

Still defining joints and parenting...

Working out leg joint parameters for the fox model...

Adding a haunch ellipsoid at the hip to fill out the thigh where it meets the body, then sizing the paw spheres to flatten and elongate slightly for a foot-like shape. Considering whether toe details are worth adding but leaning toward skipping them for simplicity.

For color, I'll keep paws the same dark tone as the socks using the cel-shaded dark paint. I'm defining the flame glow palette as icy blues and purples, and using a warm gold tone with cel shading for metallic accents instead of pulling in the full clockwork palette. I'm also considering small red tassels hanging from the bell for extra detail, and thinking about whether a crescent or halo shape would add more visual interest without overcomplicating things.

I'm debating a floating gold rune-ring halo behind the head for extra divine kitsune flair, but worried it might clash with the fanned tails, so I may skip it. Instead I'll add glowing spirit markings—making the forehead mark glow in cyan-violet using the glow function on the decal part since it's cloned with its own material, while keeping the red kumadori non-glowing, and I'm considering glowing cyan tomoe shoulder markings too for a cohesive magical effect.

I'm settling on a palette of white, red, gold, and cyan: cyan-glowing flank tomoe and forehead mark, a red dorsal stripe, and red-or-cyan tail tips, then starting to set up the TypeScript imports I'll need from the builder library and its toon/glow kits. I'm being careful to only import what I actually use since unused imports might fail typechecking, and confirming that DEG is exported from the math module so I don't need to hardcode degree-to-radian conversions myself.

Writing color and material definitions...

Still defining coat patterns...

Thinking about the tail coloring, considering whether the tip should be red or a cooler tone to contrast with the body, and how the white fur with a lavender cel shadow reads visually.

For the eyes, I'm picking an amber-gold iris to contrast against the cyan flame motif, giving the kitsune a warmer focal point. I'm also sketching a tomoe SVG shape with cyan fill, considering whether to turn it into a ring outline for a more traditional symbol look.

Now I'm adding a stroked outer ring at the right scale to frame the tomoe, then sketching a forehead flame element in red and gold tones, debating whether it should instead glow cyan to match the rest of the design's self-illuminating palette.

I'll skip glowing the forehead and just keep it a normal red-gold flame shape, then sketch a red swoosh cheek mark. Now I'm starting the builder setup, defining the hips joint as the root spine joint per spec.

Building out the spine chain, neck chain, head and jaw joints, then starting the body sweep curve through the character's silhouette points.

Adding haunch and shoulder sphere parts...

Moving on to legs and paws, then building the skull using a sphere geometry scaled to fit the head bone, confirming the Part scale accepts array values based on the toon example.

Now I'm placing eye decals symmetrically on either side of the skull surface by finding hit points at specific angles, handling the case where the hit might be null, and sizing them large relative to the head radius for an anime-style wide-eyed look.

Adding small red eyebrow dot spheres embedded near the brow position, then checking the eye decal's vertical placement relative to its height offset.

Moving on to ears now, setting up a hinged joint at each side of the head with an outward-tilted direction, then extruding the ear shape from a base point near the top-side of the skull.

Still refining the inner ear outline...

Checking the remaining inner-ear vertices against the polygon edges confirms they fall inside, so the point ordering works. For the forward offset I'm confirming the thickness protrudes slightly beyond the base ear shape, and that the +Z offset direction stays consistent in model space regardless of the mirrored side, accounting for the slight y-lean in the outline.

Skipping the ear tip tuft and bevel details since the thickness and cap sizing already work out fine. I'm now sketching placement logic for cheek tufts, positioning them with small forward/down offsets scaled by index relative to the skull radius.

Checking that tuft base points stay buried within the skull sphere for good embedding, then setting their spike directions and lengths tapering by index. I'm also checking how the tuft positions at different heights overlap with the eye decal boundaries, since the first tuft row sits close to the bottom edge of the eyes.

I'll add a few cheap whiskers per side, then work on neck ruff rings and a chest ring using the ring API to place spikes outward along the body's joint frames, tilted backward for a fur-like look.

Now I'm adding a chest bib ring around the lower spine with a wider angular spread and shorter spikes, then considering a collar loop near the neck base, though I'm still working out which point along the neck path to anchor it.

I'm casting a ray from the collar centre at a forward-downward angle to find where it intersects the chest surface, then placing a small gold sphere there to form the bell, embedded slightly into the mesh.

For the dangling tassel, I'll add a thin red cone spiking downward from that same hit point as the bell, letting it sit just beneath so the bell and tassel overlap naturally at the attachment point.

For the collar beads, I'm iterating along the collar path placing alternating red and gold spheres, though I need to account for the fact that each point's orientation follows the path's tangent direction rather than pointing outward, which affects how the beads seat against the surface.

Writing the flame curve function...

For faceting the flame shape, I want flat six-sided sections with smooth shading disabled so the tube reads as faceted rather than round, confirming the sweep options support this. The glow material applies correctly across the mesh bands without conflicting naming, and the bone/base point structure should work fine for the flame's hot inner core.

I'm planning to add two smaller side tongues leaning outward from the main flame for the tail tip, plus floating wisps and a scattering of tiny embers using small octahedron shapes with glow, randomly positioned in a bounded volume while avoiding overlap with the main flame body.

Writing tail curve math...

Still computing tail geometry...

I can get the ring's radius by sampling the sweep at t=0.2 and adding a small offset, then placing the torus geometry at that point with the chain's tangent as orientation, though I need to double check whether a ChainPoint works directly as a frame reference.

For the flame, I'll position it just past the tail tip by extending slightly beyond the last chain point along its tangent, attaching it to the final joint, and leaning it outward based on yaw for a natural flicker effect.

I'm adding spirit wisps circling at varying heights, then double-checking the overall rig structure: legs positioned correctly outward, and verifying the joint count adds up across spine, head, limbs, and tail segments to 59 total, with parts for each tail including sweeps, toruses, and flame pieces.

Tallying triangle counts across the tail sweep rings, skull sphere, and other detail meshes to estimate total scene complexity stays within reason. I'm also sanity-checking the API calls for sweeps, bezier curves, and rings to make sure arguments and types line up correctly, including defining the flame function as a closure inside the build step.

Checking the ring and along-path API signatures against SDK examples, confirming the limb import comes from the single SDK entry point, verifying the stick function's parameter order, and making sure the rng helper returns a callable random function for positioning wisps, plus flagging flat shading for faceted parts.

Now I'm working through decal placement, confirming decals target a surface object like in the toon doc examples, and figuring out ray-casting from the body surface to position a flank decal with mirroring for symmetry.

I'm checking that the chest and leg positions don't conflict with the haunch sphere coverage, then verifying whether the flank tomoe decal's glow effect will actually apply given its material type.

Now I'm adding the jaw with fangs, nose, and whiskers—looping through each side to position whisker strands radiating outward and slightly downward from the muzzle.

Confirming the rod helper's signature works with a radius array and bone sides, then checking the nose sphere geometry attaches correctly to the head bone.

Now I'm placing fangs as small cones near the lower jaw, verifying they won't overlap or get hidden by the jaw geometry since the upper jaw's bottom edge sits close to the fang's vertical span.

So fang placement works out, visible length around .015 which is fine. Now I'm thinking about color variety for rendering, maybe adding a subtle crown of small tufts to the head, and planning the forelegs next.

Positioning floating flame wisps and glow orbs around the head, placing seven of them at various angles and heights so they hover near the muzzle without clipping into the face geometry.

I need embers to avoid spawning inside the fox's body, so I'm adding a rejection check that skips positions too close to the center, retrying with a while loop until I get enough valid ember positions. I also want to double check the glow import path is correct, and I'm considering whether to add a kitsune mask element somewhere on the head.

Setting up imports for the builder, toon kit, and glow kit, and confirming the module-level texture setup will work correctly at import time.

Thinking through the ear outline typing—whether to import an OutlinePoint type or just let TypeScript infer the tuple shape inline to avoid import risk.

Now I'm sketching the leg-building loop, computing front limb joint positions per side and chaining them into shoulder/elbow/wrist joints under the spine parent.

For the chain with a tip joint, the sweep should cover the whole path, and I need a contact point on the floor for ground alignment. I'm placing a paw sphere at the end joint with a flattened scale, but checking whether the target height lines up against the sweep radius at the bottom.

Checking the math: the paw's half height and width line up with the leg end position, and the z-scaling of 1.45 covers the correct range including the leg end point. I confirm the limb's joints array already includes the tip joint, so I can just use the last joint directly.

Now for the hind limb, I'm defining a similar limb chain with its own root, target, segment lengths, and bend directions, reasoning through whether the solved pose gives plausible knee-forward, hock-back geometry despite the awkward "bends" semantics.

Checking the hind paw position and radii tapering down the leg, I verify the knee doesn't clip through the belly since it lands below the body's bottom boundary. Satisfied that's fine, I move on to the tail, planning gold-colored cuff rings and a flame-tipped tail, then start thinking through the spike helper function signature for the head spikes, confirming it takes a base point, direction, length, radius, and options including color and bone binding, and deciding no horn or extra dorsal tuft is needed beyond that.

I'm double-checking the collar loop and skin-around calls take the right point types, confirming the body sweep's paint coloring logic evaluates correctly per-point, and skipping the mouth/tongue detail. I also confirm bones like hips can be passed into part-creation calls for embers and glowing elements, and I'm now sketching out a flame helper function's parameters, debating how to type the bone argument without importing extra types.

For the bone type, I decide to reference the existing joint variable's type directly rather than importing a separate Joint type, which sidesteps any export risk. I confirm the skinned tails use point caps, the skull gets a small sphere stick detail, and the tail cuff and ring/bead alternation logic check out, including verifying tangent vectors feed correctly into the direction parameter. Writing final code now.
